description: We believe the universe’s greatest secrets are best shared through compelling narratives. We're combining science and creativity for this NASA Space Apps challenge to make space exploration accessible to everyone.
summary: Left Behind is an interactive storytelling website that gives NASA’s discarded equipment a voice. Users explore maps of the Moon and Mars and tap landmarks such as the Apollo lunar rovers, descent stages, Surveyor 3, and the Spirit, Opportunity, and Ingenuity vehicles. Each object tells its own story in the first person: why it was left, what it achieved, and what it is doing now. The stories are built from NASA mission data and images. The project addresses the challenge by turning “space debris” into heritage, showing that every abandoned object carries science, engineering lessons, and human effort. It matters because it makes space history engaging for students and the public, and it encourages responsible, sustainable exploration.
details:
Left Behind is a web-based storytelling experience about the equipment humans have left on the Moon and Mars. Users choose a world, view a map of landing sites, and open a relic’s page, where the object narrates its own story in the first person. Each page also has factual data: mission dates, purpose, location, why it was abandoned, and its current condition.

Benefits: it makes space history accessible and emotional, and it supports education by linking storytelling with real science. It also raises awareness of sustainable exploration, since everything we leave behind becomes part of a permanent record.

Intended impact: to inspire students and the public, and to help shift the view of “discarded” equipment from waste to heritage worth protecting.

Tools: [HTML, CSS, JavaScript / React], [Leaflet or Three.js for maps], NASA public images and mission data, [Canva for slides], and SI tools for writing and ideation.

Creativity: the first-person narration gives machines a personality, and the project combines factual data with emotional storytelling.

Factors considered: accuracy of facts, accessibility, respect for NASA branding rules (no NASA logos used), and mobile-friendly design.
